saturation_history.rationale: The taxonomy covers session termination through Credential and Session Expiration Policy; all Observer-based rental, bike-status, availability-list, and usage-history updates through Real-Time Status Notification; and modular bank-account/card provider integration through Payment Integration Abstraction. However, it has no dimension for rental-pricing variability, nor for notification timing and scheduled rental-lifecycle monitoring. It also lacks an axis for registration-data collection and handling, including the categories of personal, credential, and optional location data and their associated registration-security treatment. These concerns are distinct from authentication factors, encryption at rest/in transit, retention, location filtering, and payment-service structure.

uncovered_concepts: Repository pattern for bike data persistence
saturation_history.rationale: Most open codes are covered: authentication and verification-code validity map to Authentication Factor and Credential and Session Expiration Policy; credential transmission and storage map to Data Protection Scope; rental state-machine and scheduler decisions map to Rental Operation Design; payment adapters and a common provider interface map to Payment Integration Structure; and proximity queries map to Bike Availability Discovery and Notification. However, the taxonomy does not clearly capture the architectural approach for maintaining real-time bike locations, which is distinct from discovering nearby bikes or notifying availability changes. It also lacks a data-persistence/data-access dimension for Repository-based storage and usage-statistics querying. Verification-code generation and delivery can be treated as part of the authentication mechanism, while the duplicate 30-minute validity codes are already covered by the expiration-policy dimension.

uncovered_concepts: Event-driven architecture for bike lifecycle automation
saturation_history.rationale: The 30-minute verification-code TTL and verification-code expiration are covered by the existing Verification-Code Validity Policy (dimension 3). The monitoring dashboard, usage aggregation, and operational-visibility interface introduce an operational observability and fleet-monitoring concern that is not captured by the existing notification, location, or persistence dimensions. Builder-based report assembly introduces a report-generation/construction concern not represented by the current taxonomy. Finally, event-driven fleet-lifecycle automation, the bike-registration event trigger, and the resulting automated bike-removal workflow concern event-triggered operational orchestration rather than rider notifications or rental workflow state management; no existing dimension captures that axis without conflation.

Usage Data Access and Reporting is outside the stated use case's decision scope. The use case requires real-time bike-location tracking and rental operations, but does not require usage-statistics querying, downloadable usage reports, or reporting architecture. Its persistence and report-assembly alternatives therefore cannot directly change a CityBike architecture decision for this use case.

criteria.name: Orthogonality
criteria.description: Every dimension is a distinct decision point: no two dimensions ask the same question, and no dimension's candidate decisions are really options of another dimension.
criteria.reason: The dimensions generally ask distinct architectural questions: bike discovery/tracking (18) covers proximity and location tracking, status propagation (10) covers notifications, rental representation (7) covers workflow modeling, and timing/scheduling (17) covers duration-based triggers. Payment organization (5), encryption scope (4), registration collection (11), registration privacy handling (15), authentication (1), session termination (2), and verification-code validity (3) also address different concerns. The only minor proximity is between the broad registration-data security safeguard value 15.1 and encryption scope 4, but their primary questions remain distinguishable; no clear dimension pair requires merging.

criteria.name: Clarity
criteria.description: Dimension names and descriptions make the decision question clear, and value labels and descriptions make the alternatives distinguishable, so a reader could tell which dimension and value a passage about a design decision belongs to.
criteria.reason: Most dimensions clearly state their axes and most values are distinguishable, such as in 4 (in-transit versus at-rest encryption), 11 (personal, credential, and optional location collection), and 18 (proximity filtering versus real-time tracking). The main ambiguity is in 7: values 7.2 (state-machine-based rental workflow) and 7.3 (state-pattern rental lifecycle management) both describe representing the same rental stages; rename or rewrite them to distinguish workflow coordination from lifecycle state representation, or merge them. In 10, values 10.1 and 10.2 overlap because rental-state changes can be bike-status changes; clarify 10.1 as physical/availability telemetry and 10.2 as rental lifecycle events. In 17, values 17.2 and 17.3 both describe time-triggered rental notifications, so merge them or make one specifically pre-expiry scheduling and the other a different notification trigger.

criteria.name: Completeness
criteria.description: The taxonomy contains the major decision points implied by the use case, each with its main candidate decisions.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy covers bike tracking (18), payment organization (5), rental workflow and QR-related lifecycle behavior (7), encryption (4), authentication (1), and notification mechanisms (10), with multiple candidates in each. However, major use-case areas have no decision points: service decomposition, API gateway/request routing, service discovery, observability/distributed tracing, and GDPR/Privacy Directive/ISO 27001 or regional compliance mechanisms. Dimension 5 should be split or reorganized into external provider integration versus internal payment organization, using its existing adapter/interface and facade/strategy values; dimension 15 should be renamed or reorganized around the existing privacy-handling values rather than implying full regulatory-compliance coverage. The absent infrastructure and compliance areas remain substantial gaps.

criteria.name: Use case alignment
criteria.description: Every dimension serves the stated use case; none is out of its scope.
criteria.reason: Most dimensions concern CityBike’s stated architecture scope, including bike location tracking (18), payment-provider integration (5), encryption (4), authentication and session security (1, 2), privacy and registration data (11, 15), rental workflow (7), status notifications (10), and rental scheduling (17). The main weakness is that dimensions 3 (Verification-Code Validity Policy), 11 (Registration Data Collection), and parts of 2 (Session Termination Policy) emphasize fine-grained product or operational policies rather than architectural mechanisms; revise by merging these policy dimensions into the broader authentication/privacy dimensions, or move their policy values into those dimensions. The output does not need additional dimensions for omitted technologies because this criterion concerns only scope.

criteria.name: No catch-alls
criteria.description: No dimension or value is a vague catch-all ('Other', 'Miscellaneous', 'General', 'Other approaches').
criteria.reason: No catch-all dimensions or values are present. Each dimension is framed around a specific CityBike concern, such as bike location tracking (18), payment organization (5), encryption scope (4), authentication (1), and rental timing (17), and the values describe concrete alternatives or outcomes rather than buckets like 'Other' or 'Miscellaneous'. No revision is needed for the catch-all criterion.

criteria.name: Axis vs. value
criteria.description: Each dimension is a decision point with alternatives, not a single option presented as a dimension; each value is an option, not a sub-topic.
criteria.reason: Several entries do not represent one decision with alternative answers. Dimension 18, "Bike Location Discovery and Tracking," combines proximity filtering (18.1) with the separate tracking-service choice (18.2); separate or drop one axis rather than treating them as alternatives. Dimension 11, "Registration Data Collection," lists independently collectable data categories (11.1–11.3), not alternative collection strategies; reorganize these as outcomes or remove the dimension. Dimension 15, "Registration Privacy Handling," mixes general safeguards (15.1) with biometric deletion (15.2), which are distinct privacy-lifecycle decisions; separate or relocate the deletion entry. Dimension 10, "Bike Status Notification," mixes notification mechanisms, subjects, and outcomes: move 10.3 and 10.4 out of the candidate values as outcomes and keep only a single notification decision axis. criteria.reason: The taxonomy places 18 of 20 decision-bearing passages, covering registration fields and safeguards (11), 15-minute timeout and manual logout (2), 30-minute verification validity and expiration (3), authentication (1), encryption (4), payment facade/adapters (5), rental state and command patterns (7), observers and bike proximity filtering (9–10), and timing notifications (8). The unplaced passages are 4a925776-d050-43c1-9bb1-54800ab7e7b6, which decides to use the Builder pattern for usage-history report assembly; add a value for usage-history report construction, supported by that passage. Also unplaced is 59e2c235-89e7-4eaf-80f4-8019e9db1a9d, which decides to use Strategy for rental pricing calculations while excluding notification timing; add a rental-pricing strategy value/dimension rather than relying on payment-provider value 5.2.

criteria.name: Candidate-decision coverage
criteria.description: The options that the sampled passages adopt or reject are named as values (candidate decisions) of the right dimension.
criteria.reason: Most adopted options are named, including 15-minute inactivity termination and manual logout in dimension 2, 30-minute code validity in dimension 3, authentication methods in dimension 1, encryption in dimension 4, payment adapters/facade in dimension 5, rental states and observers, and proximity filtering. Missing options are: add a report-construction dimension and value "Builder-based usage-history report assembly" for 4a925776-d050-43c1-9bb1-54800ab7e7b6; add a rental-pricing dimension and value "Strategy-based rental pricing calculation" for 59e2c235-89e7-4eaf-80f4-8019e9db1a9d; add a rejected value "Command-based notification scheduling" to dimension 8, Rental Timing Notification, for 7e4e475d-ce53-4e3a-8cd1-e4a58c392fd0; and add a rejected value "Strategy-based notification timing" to dimension 8 for 59e2c235-89e7-4eaf-80f4-8019e9db1a9d.

criteria.name: Orthogonality
criteria.description: Every dimension is a distinct decision point: no two dimensions ask the same question, and no dimension's candidate decisions are really options of another dimension.
criteria.reason: Most dimensions ask distinct questions, such as authentication (1), session termination (2), verification-code validity (3), payment organization versus provider integration (5 and 6), and code handling (13). The main overlap is between Usage Data Access and Reporting (12) and Operational Monitoring Interface (14): both include usage-data aggregation and reporting-oriented views, so merge them or move the overlapping aggregation/report values into one dimension. Registration Privacy Handling (15) also partially overlaps Data Encryption Scope (4), especially the broad 'Registration-data security safeguards' value (15.1); narrow 15 to privacy lifecycle/deletion or move/remove that broad safeguard value. Bike Information Propagation (10) and Operational Monitoring Interface (14) have a lesser overlap through real-time status dashboards and monitoring, which should be separated by moving dashboard-specific values to 14 and retaining only distribution mechanisms in 10.

criteria.name: Clarity
criteria.description: Dimension names and descriptions make the decision question clear, and value labels and descriptions make the alternatives distinguishable, so a reader could tell which dimension and value a passage about a design decision belongs to.
criteria.reason: Most dimensions have clear decision questions and their values are described distinctly, such as Authentication Mechanism (1) and Payment Provider Integration (6), with useful specificity for CityBike payment and 1000-meter bike-location behavior. The main weaknesses are naming and value fit: rename Verification-Code Validity Policy (3) to include enforcement because value 3.3 is an enforcement mechanism rather than a validity window; merge credential-specific values 4.3 and 4.4 into the broader in-transit and at-rest values because they substantially overlap 4.1 and 4.2; drop or replace the vague Operational visibility interface value (14.3), which is not distinguishable from the dashboard and aggregation values; and drop or sharpen Scheduler-triggered time-based notifications (7.6), which overlaps the more specific pre-expiry notification value 7.5.

criteria.name: Completeness
criteria.description: The taxonomy contains the major decision points implied by the use case, each with its main candidate decisions.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy covers several use-case areas with multiple candidates, including Authentication Mechanism (1), Data Encryption Scope (4), Payment Provider Integration (6), Rental Workflow Coordination (7), and bike location/proximity handling in Bike Information Propagation (10). However, major architectural decision areas are not represented: service decomposition, API gateway/request routing, container orchestration, service discovery, regulatory-compliance mechanisms, and observability/distributed tracing. Reorganize existing content by splitting dimension 10 into separate bike-location tracking and real-time propagation questions, and split dimension 7 into workflow coordination versus scheduling so each retains at least two candidates. Dimensions 14 Operational Monitoring Interface and 15 Registration Privacy Handling should be renamed/reframed around observability and compliance only if their existing values genuinely support those axes; otherwise the current values do not provide candidate decisions for those missing areas. The existing dimensions also focus heavily on application behavior and design patterns rather than the platform and integration choices emphasized by the CityBike parameters.

criteria.name: Use case alignment
criteria.description: Every dimension serves the stated use case; none is out of its scope.
criteria.reason: Most dimensions are relevant to CityBike's stated architecture concerns: authentication (1), encryption and privacy (4, 15), payment integration and organization (5, 6), rental and QR-unlock workflow (7), real-time bike location and proximity handling (10), and event automation (16). However, dimension 2, Session Termination Policy, and dimension 3, Verification-Code Validity Policy, are narrow timing/configuration policies rather than architectural variation; merge their content into dimensions 1 and 13 or drop them. Dimension 11, Registration Data Collection, is primarily a data-collection requirement; merge it with dimension 15, Registration Privacy Handling. Dimensions 12, Usage Data Access and Reporting, and 14, Operational Monitoring Interface, are only tangentially related to the use case's real-time tracking and observability concerns; merge their directly operational content into dimension 10 or drop the remaining reporting/UI-specific values.

criteria.name: No catch-alls
criteria.description: No dimension or value is a vague catch-all ('Other', 'Miscellaneous', 'General', 'Other approaches').
criteria.reason: Most dimensions and values are specific alternatives rather than catch-all buckets. Two broad items should be tightened: value 15.1, "Registration-data security safeguards," uses a generic safeguards bucket and should be dropped or merged into the more specific encryption dimension 4; value 14.3, "Operational visibility interface," is a vague residual category and should be dropped, since dimensions 14.1 and 14.2 already specify the dashboard and aggregation mechanisms.

criteria.name: Axis vs. value
criteria.description: Each dimension is a decision point with alternatives, not a single option presented as a dimension; each value is an option, not a sub-topic.
criteria.reason: Several dimensions mix decisions with subtopics or implementation details. Split dimension 7, "Rental Workflow Coordination," into workflow representation (7.1–7.3) and timing/notification scheduling (7.4–7.6). Split dimension 10, "Bike Information Propagation," so location tracking and proximity handling (10.5–10.7), which directly address CityBike's real-time and 1000-meter location requirement, are separate from status notification (10.1–10.4). In dimension 4, "Data Encryption Scope," merge or remove 4.3 and 4.4 because credential transmission/storage are narrower instances of 4.1 and 4.2. In dimension 13, "Verification-Code Handling," merge 13.1 and 13.2 into one handling decision because generation and delivery are workflow stages rather than alternative answers. In dimension 16, "Fleet Event Automation," drop or merge 16.2 and 16.3 into 16.1 because the registration trigger and removal workflow are subtopics of event-driven automation, not peer alternatives.

criteria.name: One decision point
criteria.description: Each dimension is a single decision point: all its candidate decisions are alternative answers to one question, rather than a broad topic bundling several questions. Where the use case names quality attributes or forces, dimensions whose choice is driven by recognizable quality attributes or trade-offs are preferred (quality-attribute grounding).
criteria.reason: Several dimensions are coherent and have at least two candidates, such as Authentication Mechanism (1), Payment Provider Integration (6), and Registration Data Collection (11), with some relevance to CityBike's security, privacy, and payment concerns. However, Rental Workflow Coordination (7) mixes command/state workflow choices with scheduling and notifications; split it into workflow coordination (7.1–7.3) and rental timing/notification scheduling (7.4–7.6). Bike Information Propagation (10) mixes event propagation with location tracking and proximity queries; split it into notification propagation (10.1–10.4) and location discovery/tracking (10.5–10.7). Verification-Code Validity Policy (3) includes the non-alternative enforcement value 3.3 alongside duration choices; move or drop 3.3 so the dimension contains only validity alternatives. Data Encryption Scope (4) mixes general transport/storage scope with credential-specific scope; split 4.1–4.2 from 4.3–4.4. Fleet Event Automation (16) also includes 16.3, an automated result rather than a candidate decision, so reclassify it as an outcome or drop it, leaving the event-trigger alternatives.

Dimension 18, "Bike Location Discovery and Tracking," combines proximity filtering (18.1) with the separate tracking-service choice (18.2); separate or drop one axis rather than treating them as alternatives. Dimension 11, "Registration Data Collection," lists independently collectable data categories (11.1–11.3), not alternative collection strategies; reorganize these as outcomes or remove the dimension. Dimension 15, "Registration Privacy Handling," mixes general safeguards (15.1) with biometric deletion (15.2), which are distinct privacy-lifecycle decisions; separate or relocate the deletion entry. Dimension 10, "Bike Status Notification," mixes notification mechanisms, subjects, and outcomes: move 10.3 and 10.4 out of the candidate values as outcomes and keep only a single notification decision axis. Dimension 17, "Rental Timing and Notification Scheduling," similarly combines duration monitoring, pre-expiry scheduling, and notification triggering; reorganize these into one decision axis or drop the non-alternative entries. These issues are especially significant given the use case's explicit requirements for real-time bike tracking, rental notifications, and privacy handling.

Id 3 also combines validity duration with expiration enforcement. These issues are significant despite the use case's clear security, privacy, GDPR, and real-time-tracking concerns; dimensions such as id 1, id 2, and id 4 are comparatively coherent and have at least two candidates.
